mainTopic: How the רבנן and רבי שמעון read the ציצית פסוקים, followed by praises of ציצית and the other מצוות, and רבי מאיר's teachings on daily ברכות.
overview: The גמרא first asks what the רבנן learn from ״אשר תכסה בה״. They use it to include a five-cornered garment in ציצית, while ״על ארבע״ leaves out a three-cornered one, since five contains four but three does not. רבי שמעון learns the five-cornered rule from the single word ״אשר״ instead. Next the גמרא asks what the רבנן learn from ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״. A series of ברייתות read it as a reminder of קריאת שמע and of כלאים, as making ציצית equal to all the מצוות, and as a chain of seeing, remembering and doing. רבי שמעון בר יוחאי adds that being careful with ציצית brings a person to greet the שכינה. The גמרא then praises the מצוות that surround a Jew: תפילין, ציצית, מזוזה, and דוד's comfort in his מילה. רבי מאיר explains why תכלת was chosen and why leaving out white strings is punished more. He also teaches 100 daily ברכות and three daily ברכות. The amud ends as רב אחא בר יעקב starts to answer his son about which third ברכה to say, and his answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: What do the רבנן learn from 'With which you cover yourself'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the רבנן use the phrase ״אשר תכסה בה״.
steps.simpleTranslation: This phrase, 'with which you cover yourself' — what do the רבנן do with it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the רבנן learn from the words ״אשר תכסה בה״. This question sets up the next step, where the answer is given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier on the daf, רבי שמעון used this phrase for his own teaching. Every phrase in the תורה should teach something. So the גמרא wants to know what the רבנן, who disagree with him, learn from these words.

keyTerms.meaning: What do they do with it? (How do they use this verse?)

phrases.english: This phrase, 'with which you cover yourself'
phrases.notes: דברים 22:12. The question is about the רבנן, who disagreed with רבי שמעון just before this.

phrases.english: what do they do with it?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי אֲשֶׁר תְּכַסֶּה בָּהּ מַאי עָבְדִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the earlier part of the daf, where רבי שמעון used this phrase for his own teaching.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the רבנן learn from ״אשר תכסה בה״.

steps.title: Four corners, not three
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן need the phrase for a teaching in a ברייתא. The ברייתא opens by saying that ״על ארבע כנפות״ means four corners and not three.
steps.simpleTranslation: They need it for what was taught in a ברייתא: 'On the four corners of your garment' means four, and not three.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן need the phrase for a ברייתא. The ברייתא starts by saying that a garment with three corners does not need ציצית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'four corners' give a minimum: a three-cornered garment is exempt. The role of ״אשר תכסה בה״ is not shown yet. It comes in the next part of the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: They need it (for a different teaching)

phrases.english: They need it for that which was taught in a ברייתא:
'On the four corners of your garment' —
phrases.notes: דברים 22:12, the same פסוק.

phrases.english: four, and not three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1 by bringing a ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן use the phrase as part of a ברייתא about how many corners a garment needs.

steps.title: Five corners are included by 'with which you cover yourself'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks whether 'four' might exclude five instead of three. It answers that ״אשר תכסה בה״ includes a five-cornered garment, so 'four' must be excluding three.
steps.simpleTranslation: You say 'four and not three.' But maybe it means 'four and not five'? When the פסוק says 'with which you cover yourself,' a five-cornered garment is already included. So how do I explain 'on the four'? Four and not three.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks whether 'four' could be shutting out a five-cornered garment. It then shows that ״אשר תכסה בה״ brings five-cornered garments in, so 'four' must be shutting out three.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Four' could have been read as 'exactly four,' which would exclude both three and five. The phrase ״אשר תכסה בה״ covers any garment you wear, so it brings in five. That leaves 'four' with one job only: excluding three. This is how the רבנן use the phrase.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps it only means... (testing another possible reading)
So how do I explain (the other words)?

steps.whatToRemember: ״אשר תכסה בה״ includes five corners. ״על ארבע״ excludes three corners.

phrases.english: You say four and not three,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא אַרְבַּע וְלֹא חָמֵשׁ?
phrases.english: or perhaps it means only four and not five?
When it says 'with which you cover yourself,'
a garment with five corners is already mentioned,
so how do I explain 'on the four'?
Four and not three.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר אַרְבַּע וְלֹא שָׁלֹשׁ אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא אַרְבַּע וְלֹא חָמֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא and shows where ״אשר תכסה בה״ comes in.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A five-cornered garment needs ציצית because of ״אשר תכסה בה״. A three-cornered garment is exempt because of ״על ארבע״.

steps.title: Why include five and exclude three?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks why we include five and exclude three, and not the other way around.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what did you see to include a five-cornered garment and exclude a three-cornered one?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks why the rule goes this way and not the reverse. This question sets up the reasoning in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In theory, ״אשר תכסה בה״ could include three corners while 'four' excludes five. The ברייתא needs a reason to choose one reading over the other.

keyTerms.meaning: What did you see? (Why did you choose this way?)

phrases.english: And what did you see to include a five-cornered garment
and to exclude a three-cornered garment?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָה רָאִיתָ לְרַבּוֹת בַּעֲלַת חָמֵשׁ וּלְהוֹצִיא בַּעֲלַת שָׁלֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the direction of the reading given in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason for including five and excluding three, and not the reverse.

steps.title: Five contains four; three does not
steps.stepSummary: Five corners contain four, so a five-cornered garment fits 'four corners.' Three corners do not reach four, so a three-cornered garment does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: I include a five-cornered garment, because five contains four. I exclude a three-cornered garment, because three does not contain four.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains its choice. A five-cornered garment still has four corners. A three-cornered garment does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'four corners' are true of a five-cornered garment, since it has four corners plus one more. A three-cornered garment is missing a corner, so it can never fit the פסוק. That is why the including phrase goes with five and the excluding phrase goes with three.
steps.whatToRemember: Five corners already contain four, so they qualify. Three corners do not reach four, so they do not.

phrases.english: I include a five-cornered garment,
since five contains four,
and I exclude a three-cornered garment,
since three does not contain four.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְרַבֶּה אֲנִי בַּעֲלַת חָמֵשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בִּכְלַל חָמֵשׁ אַרְבַּע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Five contains four, but three does not. So five is included and three is excluded.

steps.title: רבי שמעון learns five corners from the word 'which'
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון needs the full phrase for something else. He learns that a five-cornered garment needs ציצית from the single word ״אשר״.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי שמעון? He learns it from the word 'which.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how רבי שמעון knows that a five-cornered garment needs ציצית, since he used the phrase for his own teaching. The answer is that he learns it from the extra word ״אשר״.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון already used ״אשר תכסה בה״ for a different teaching. So he needs another source for five corners. He finds it in the extra word ״אשר״ by itself.

keyTerms.meaning: It comes out from; he learns it from
'Which', an extra word in the פסוק

phrases.english: And רבי שמעון,
phrases.notes: This is a short question: where does he learn the five-cornered rule, since he used the phrase for his own teaching?

phrases.english: he learns it from the word 'which.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to רבי שמעון's source for the five-cornered rule.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי שמעון learns it from the extra word ״אשר״.

steps.title: The רבנן do not learn from 'which'
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן do not learn anything from the single word ״אשר״. That is why they need the whole phrase for the five-cornered rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן? They do not learn anything from the word 'which.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the רבנן do not use ״אשר״ the way רבי שמעון does. They do not read any teaching into that single word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the root of the disagreement. רבי שמעון learns from the extra word ״אשר״, so the full phrase is free for his other teaching. The רבנן do not learn from ״אשר״, so they need the whole phrase to include a five-cornered garment.

keyTerms.meaning: It does not mean anything to them (they do not learn from it)

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree that a five-cornered garment needs ציצית. They only disagree about the source: the רבנן use the whole phrase ״אשר תכסה בה״, and רבי שמעון uses the word ״אשר״.

phrases.english: And the רבנן?
They do not learn anything from the word 'which.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the רבנן do not follow רבי שמעון's reading of ״אשר״.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The disagreement is only about the source. The רבנן do not learn from ״אשר״, so they use the full phrase. רבי שמעון does learn from ״אשר״.

steps.title: What do the רבנן learn from 'and you shall see it'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the רבנן do with the words ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״, since they do not use them the way רבי שמעון does.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן, what do they do with this phrase ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the רבנן and asks what they learn from the phrase ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״. This question sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון read ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״ as 'something you can see,' so night clothing is exempt. The רבנן do not learn that, so the גמרא wants to know what lesson they take from these words. The Torah does not use extra words for nothing, so they must teach something.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And you shall see it.' Words from the ציצית פסוק

phrases.english: And the Rabbis, this phrase "that you may look upon it"
phrases.notes: במדבר 15:39. רבי שמעון learned from these words that night clothing is exempt from ציצית.

phrases.english: what do they do with it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן, הַאי ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״ מַאי עָבְדִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 7 explained why the רבנן need the whole phrase for the five-cornered garment. Now the גמרא asks how the רבנן use the other phrase that רבי שמעון relied on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the רבנן learn from ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״, since they do not use it to exempt night garments.

steps.title: Seeing ציצית reminds us of קריאת שמע
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן use the phrase for a ברייתא: seeing ציצית should remind you of a מצוה that depends on it, namely קריאת שמע. The morning שמע starts once you can tell the תכלת apart from the white strings.
steps.simpleTranslation: They need it for what a ברייתא teaches. 'And you shall see it and remember' means: see this מצוה and remember another מצוה that depends on it. Which one? קריאת שמע. As the משנה says: from when may one say שמע in the morning? From when one can tell apart the blue from the white.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן use ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״ for a different lesson: seeing ציצית reminds you of קריאת שמע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The time for the morning שמע is set by when there is enough light to tell the תכלת strings from the white strings. So קריאת שמע 'hangs on' ציצית, and seeing the ציצית links you to it. That is how the רבנן use the phrase, instead of using it to exempt night clothing.

keyTerms.meaning: The special sky-blue dye used for some ציצית strings

phrases.english: They need it for that which is taught in a baraita:
"That you may look upon it and remember"
see this מצוה
and remember another מצוה
that is contingent on it.
phrases.notes: Some versions say בּוֹ, in round brackets. The corrected wording is בָּהּ, in square brackets.

phrases.english: And which is that? It is the recitation of Shema.

phrases.aramaic: דִּתְנַן: מֵאֵימָתַי קוֹרִין אֶת שְׁמַע בְּשַׁחֲרִית?
phrases.english: As we learned: From when may one recite Shema in the morning?
phrases.notes: This is the משנה in ברכות 9b.

phrases.english: From when one can distinguish between sky-blue and white.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן use ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ וּזְכַרְתֶּם״ to teach that seeing ציצית reminds you of קריאת שמע. The morning שמע depends on being able to see the difference between תכלת and white.

steps.title: Seeing ציצית reminds us of כלאים
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא reads the same words differently: seeing ציצית reminds you of the מצוה right next to it in the Torah, the ban on כלאים (wool and linen together).
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'And you shall see it and remember' means: see this מצוה and remember another מצוה placed right next to it. Which one? כלאים, as it says: 'Do not wear שעטנז, wool and linen together. Make for yourself twisted cords.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא that links seeing ציצית to a different מצוה: the ban on כלאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the link is not about timing. It is about where the מצוות are placed in the Torah. In ספר דברים, the ban on שעטנז is followed right away by the מצוה of גדילים (ציצית), so the two are 'next to each other.'

keyTerms.meaning: That is right next to it (in the Torah)
Forbidden mixtures. Here, wool and linen in one garment
A garment of wool and linen mixed together
Twisted cords. Another Torah word for ציצית

phrases.english: And it is taught in another baraita:
"That you may look upon it and remember":
see this מצוה
and remember another מצוה that is adjacent to it.
And which is that? It is the מצוה of diverse kinds,
as it is written: "You shall not wear diverse kinds,
wool and linen together.
You shall prepare yourself twisted cords."
phrases.notes: דברים 22:11–12. The very next פסוק after שעטנז is about ציצית.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second reading of ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ וּזְכַרְתֶּם״, linking it to כלאים instead of קריאת שמע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seeing ציצית should remind a person of the ban on כלאים, which sits right next to ציצית in the Torah.

steps.title: Whoever is obligated in ציצית is obligated in all מצוות
steps.stepSummary: A third ברייתא learns from 'and remember all the מצוות of ה׳' that once a person is obligated in ציצית, he is obligated in all the מצוות. The גמרא says this follows רבי שמעון, who holds ציצית is a time-bound מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'And you shall see it and remember all the מצוות of ה׳.' Once a person is obligated in this מצוה, he is obligated in all the מצוות. This follows רבי שמעון, who says ציצית is a positive מצוה caused by time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third ברייתא. Then it adds a short note telling us which תנא's view this ברייתא follows: רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי שמעון, ציצית is a מצות עשה שהזמן גרמא (day only, not night), so women are exempt from it. That means only those obligated in every מצוה, including time-bound ones, are obligated in ציצית. So 'obligated in ציצית' really means 'obligated in all the מצוות.'

keyTerms.meaning: A positive מצוה that depends on time. Women are exempt from these.

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean women have no מצוות at all. It means that whoever is obligated in ציצית (according to רבי שמעון, only men) is also obligated in every מצוה, including the time-bound ones.

phrases.english: It is taught in another baraita:
"That you may look upon it and remember
all the commandments of the Lord":
once a person is obligated in this מצוה,
he is obligated in all of the מצוות.
And this is the opinion of Rabbi Shimon,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה שֶׁהַזְּמַן גְּרָמָאּ הִיא.
phrases.english: who says: it is a positive, time-bound מצוה.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ וּזְכַרְתֶּם אֶת כׇּל מִצְוֹת ה׳״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third reading of the פסוק. It focuses on the words 'all the מצוות of ה׳,' and the גמרא names whose view it follows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whoever is obligated in ציצית is obligated in all the מצוות. This fits רבי שמעון's view that ציצית is time-bound.

steps.title: ציצית is equal to all the מצוות
steps.stepSummary: A fourth ברייתא learns from the same words that the מצוה of ציצית is as weighty as all the other מצוות together.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'And you shall see it and remember all the מצוות of ה׳.' This מצוה is equal to all the מצוות together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a fourth ברייתא on this פסוק, which praises how great the מצוה of ציצית is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The step before read 'all the מצוות' as a rule about who is obligated. This ברייתא reads it as a statement of value instead. Seeing ציצית brings all the מצוות to mind, so ציצית weighs as much as all of them together.
steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן do not use ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״ to exempt night clothing. The גמרא's answer for them is the first ברייתא: seeing ציצית reminds us of קריאת שמע. The other ברייתות add more readings of the same words: ציצית reminds us of כלאים; whoever is obligated in it is obligated in all מצוות (this one follows רבי שמעון, not the רבנן); and ציצית is equal to all the מצוות. The next step adds one more lesson from the same פסוק.

phrases.english: It is taught in another baraita:

phrases.aramaic: ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ וּזְכַרְתֶּם אֶת כׇּל מִצְוֹת ה׳״,
phrases.english: "That you may look upon it and remember all the commandments of the Lord":
this מצוה is equivalent
to all the מצוות.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ וּזְכַרְתֶּם אֶת כׇּל מִצְוֹת ה׳״, שְׁקוּלָה מִצְוָה זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A fourth reading of the same words. It reads 'all the מצוות' as praise of ציצית, not as a rule about who is obligated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מצוה of ציצית is equal to all the מצוות together.

steps.title: Seeing leads to remembering, and remembering leads to doing
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא reads ״וּרְאִיתֶם... וּזְכַרְתֶּם... וַעֲשִׂיתֶם״ as a chain: seeing the ציצית leads to remembering the מצוות, and remembering leads to keeping them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'You shall see it and remember... and do.' Seeing brings a person to remember, and remembering brings a person to act.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more ברייתא on the same פסוק. This one reads the three verbs (see, remember, do) as steps that lead into each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier ברייתות used the פסוק to link ציצית to one particular מצוה, or to all the מצוות. This one explains how ציצית works: looking at it makes you remember, and remembering moves you to act.

keyTerms.meaning: Seeing; here, looking at the ציצית
Leads to; brings a person to

phrases.english: And another ברייתא teaches:
'That you may see it and remember... and do'
phrases.notes: במדבר 15:39.

phrases.english: Seeing leads to remembering,
and remembering leads to doing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a fifth ברייתא reading of the same words in the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Looking at ציצית leads to remembering the מצוות, and remembering leads to doing them.

steps.title: Whoever is careful with ציצית merits greeting the שכינה
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בר יוחאי teaches that someone who is careful with ציצית merits greeting the שכינה. He learns it from the word ״אֹתוֹ״, which appears both in the ציצית פסוק and in a פסוק about serving ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בר יוחאי says: Anyone who is careful with this מצוה earns the right to greet the שכינה. Here it says 'you shall see Him (אותו)', and there it says 'Fear ה׳ your God, and Him (אותו) you shall serve.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון בר יוחאי adds a bigger reward for ציצית. He proves it by linking the same word in two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק in דברים, ״אֹתוֹ״ clearly means ה׳. So he reads ״וּרְאִיתֶם אֹתוֹ״ in the ציצית פסוק as 'you will see Him' as well, meaning the שכינה. The reward goes to someone who is זריז, eager and careful, in this מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: Eager and careful; quick to do a מצוה
'It is written here... and it is written there': linking two פסוקים through a shared word

steps.whyThisMatters: This raises ציצית from a reminder to a path toward closeness with ה׳ himself.

phrases.english: And רבי שמעון בר יוחאי says:
Anyone who is diligent in this מצוה
merits greeting the Divine Presence.
It is written here: 'You shall see it (אותו)',
and it is written there: 'You shall fear ה׳ your God'
'and Him (אותו) shall you serve.'
phrases.notes: דברים 6:13. There, אותו means ה׳, so he reads the ציצית פסוק the same way: 'you will see Him.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A further teaching in the same ברייתא, adding a spiritual reward for ציצית.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whoever is careful with ציצית merits greeting the שכינה, based on the shared word אותו.

steps.title: Israel is beloved, surrounded by מצוות
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא praises Israel: ה׳ surrounded them with מצוות, namely תפילין on the head and arm, ציצית on their clothes, and מזוזה on their doors. דוד praised ה׳ for these 'seven times a day.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Israel is beloved, because ה׳ surrounded them with מצוות. They have תפילין on their heads, תפילין on their arms, ציצית on their clothes, and a מזוזה on their doorways. About these דוד said: 'Seven times a day I praise You for Your just laws.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from ציצית alone to a wider idea. A Jew is surrounded on every side by מצוות, and that shows ה׳'s love.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצוות listed cover the head, the arm, the body (through the clothes) and the home. 'Seven' in the פסוק is understood to count these מצוות, which is why דוד praises ה׳ seven times.

keyTerms.meaning: Leather boxes with פסוקים, worn on the head and arm
A scroll with פסוקים fixed on the doorpost

phrases.english: The Sages taught: Israel is beloved,
for the Holy One, Blessed be He, surrounded them with מצוות:
tefillin on their heads and tefillin on their arms,
and tzitzis on their garments and a mezuza for their doorways.
And about them David said:
'Seven times a day I praise You, because of Your righteous laws.'
phrases.notes: תהלים 119:164. The seven are counted as 2 תפילין, 4 corners of ציצית, and 1 מזוזה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the topic from ציצית to all the מצוות that surround a Jew.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ה׳ showed love for Israel by surrounding them with תפילין, ציצית and מזוזה.

steps.title: דוד in the bathhouse finds comfort in his מילה
steps.stepSummary: Undressed in the bathhouse, דוד was upset to be without any מצוה. Then he remembered his מילה and calmed down. Afterward he sang about it in the מזמור 'on the eighth.'
steps.simpleTranslation: When דוד went into the bathhouse and saw himself standing undressed, he said: 'Woe is me that I stand without any מצוה!' Once he remembered the מילה in his body, he calmed down. After he left, he sang a song about it, as it says: 'For the leader, on the eighth, a psalm of דוד.' This is about מילה, which is given on the eighth day.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a story about דוד. It shows that even with no תפילין, ציצית or clothing, a Jew is never without a מצוה, because the מילה is in his body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the bathhouse all the outer מצוות are gone, and that frightened דוד. The מילה stays on the body always, so it surrounds a Jew even when nothing else does. The word ״הַשְּׁמִינִית״ (the eighth) is read as a hint to מילה on the eighth day.

keyTerms.meaning: His mind was settled; he calmed down
'The eighth'; read here as a hint to מילה on the eighth day

phrases.english: And when David entered the bathhouse
and saw himself standing undressed, he said:

phrases.aramaic: אוֹי לִי שֶׁאֶעֱמוֹד עָרוֹם בְּלֹא מִצְוָה!
phrases.english: Woe is me, that I stand undressed without any מצוה!
But once he remembered the circumcision in his flesh,
his mind was put at ease.
After he came out, he said a song about it,
phrases.notes: 'It' means the מילה.

phrases.english: as it says: 'For the leader, on the eighth, a psalm of David,'
phrases.notes: תהלים 12:1.

phrases.english: about circumcision, which was given for the eighth day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of דוד and being surrounded by מצוות, now when the outer ones are absent.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even with no other מצוה on him, a Jew still carries the מצוה of מילה in his body.

steps.title: The מצוות guard a person from sin
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב teaches that someone with תפילין, ציצית and מזוזה is strengthened against sin. He proves it from 'a threefold cord is not quickly broken' and from 'the angel of ה׳ camps around those who fear Him.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says: Anyone who has תפילין on his head, תפילין on his arm, ציצית on his clothes and a מזוזה on his door is fully strengthened so that he will not sin. As it says: 'A threefold cord is not quickly broken.' And it also says: 'The angel of ה׳ camps around those who fear Him and rescues them.'
steps.whatsHappening: This last teaching adds a new benefit to the surrounding מצוות. Besides showing ה׳'s love, they actively protect a person from sinning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'threefold cord' is read as the three kinds of מצוות (תפילין, ציצית, מזוזה), which together are hard to break. The second פסוק adds that these מצוות surround a person like a protecting camp of angels.
steps.whatToRemember: These teachings build on each other. Seeing ציצית leads to remembering and doing. Being careful with it brings a person to the שכינה. Being surrounded by תפילין, ציצית, מזוזה and מילה shows ה׳'s love and guards a person from sin.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says:
Anyone who has tefillin on his head
and tefillin on his arm and tzitzis on his garment
and a mezuza on his doorway
is fully strengthened so that he will not sin,
as it says: 'And a threefold cord is not quickly broken,'
phrases.notes: קהלת 4:12.

phrases.aramaic: וְאוֹמֵר: ״חֹנֶה מַלְאַךְ ה׳ סָבִיב לִירֵאָיו וַיְחַלְּצֵם״.
phrases.english: and it says: 'The angel of ה׳ camps around those who fear Him, and rescues them.'
phrases.notes: תהלים 34:8.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a protective benefit to the list of surrounding מצוות from step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Being surrounded by תפילין, ציצית and מזוזה strengthens a person against sin.

steps.title: Why תכלת: its color leads the mind to the כסא הכבוד
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר explains that תכלת was chosen because its color is like the sea, the sea is like the sky, and the sky is like the כסא הכבוד, and he supports this with two פסוקים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר used to say: Why is תכלת different from all other colors? Because תכלת looks like the sea, the sea looks like the sky, and the sky looks like the כסא הכבוד. One פסוק says that under ה׳'s feet was something like sapphire brickwork, like the sky itself in clearness. Another פסוק says the throne looked like sapphire stone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא where רבי מאיר explains why the special ציצית string is colored תכלת and not some other color.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He builds a chain of resemblances: תכלת, then sea, then sky (רקיע), then the כסא הכבוד. The first פסוק ties the sky to sapphire, and the second ties sapphire to the throne. So looking at the תכלת string is meant to lift a person's thoughts all the way up to ה׳'s throne.

keyTerms.meaning: The special sky-blue dye used for one of the ציצית strings
The Throne of Glory, ה׳'s throne

steps.whyThisMatters: It continues the theme from the earlier steps: seeing the ציצית is supposed to lead a person to think about ה׳.

phrases.english: It is taught in a ברייתא: Rabbi Meir would say:
What is different about techeles
from all other kinds of colors?
Because techeles resembles the sea,
and the sea resembles the sky,
and the sky resembles the Throne of Glory,
as it is said: "And under His feet
was something like a paved work of sapphire
and like the very heavens in clearness,"
phrases.notes: שמות 24:10. This פסוק links the sky to sapphire.

phrases.english: and it is written: "Like the appearance of a sapphire stone,
the likeness of a throne."
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 1:26. This one links sapphire to the throne, which completes the chain.

steps.triggerLanguage: תניא, היה רבי מאיר אומר: מה נשתנה תכלת מכל מיני צבעונין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of praises of ציצית and מצוות, now focusing on the meaning of the תכלת color.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תכלת was chosen because its color leads, step by step, to the image of the כסא הכבוד.

steps.title: Skipping the easy white strings is punished more
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר teaches that leaving out the white strings is punished more than leaving out the תכלת, and he explains it with a parable of a king who asked for a clay seal and a gold seal.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר used to say: The punishment for leaving out the white strings is bigger than the punishment for leaving out the תכלת. A parable: A human king told two servants to bring him a seal. He told one to bring a clay seal and the other to bring a gold seal. Both failed and brought nothing. Who gets the bigger punishment? The one who was told to bring the clay seal and still did not bring it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching of רבי מאיר, explained with a parable, about which ציצית string is worse to leave out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might expect that missing the precious תכלת is worse. רבי מאיר says the opposite: white strings are cheap and easy to get, like clay, so not having them shows plain carelessness. תכלת is rare and costly, like gold, so failing to get it is more understandable.

keyTerms.meaning: White, here meaning the plain white ציצית strings
A parable, a story used to explain a point

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean white strings are more important than תכלת. It means that neglecting something easy is a bigger failure than neglecting something hard.

phrases.english: It is taught in a ברייתא: Rabbi Meir would say:
Greater is the punishment for leaving out white
than the punishment for leaving out techeles.
A parable: to what can this be compared?
To a king of flesh and blood
who spoke to his two servants.

phrases.aramaic: לְאֶחָד אָמַר: ״הָבֵא לִי חוֹתָם שֶׁל טִיט״,
phrases.english: To one he said: "Bring me a seal of clay,"

phrases.aramaic: וּלְאֶחָד אָמַר: ״הָבֵא לִי חוֹתָם שֶׁל זָהָב״,
phrases.english: and to the other he said: "Bring me a seal of gold."
Both were negligent and did not bring them.
Which of them gets the greater punishment?
You must say: the one to whom he said

phrases.aramaic: ״הָבֵא לִי חוֹתָם שֶׁל טִיט״ וְלֹא הֵבִיא.
phrases.english: "Bring me a seal of clay," and he did not bring it.

steps.triggerLanguage: תניא, היה רבי מאיר אומר: גדול עונשו של לבן יותר מעונשו של תכלת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After praising תכלת, רבי מאיר teaches that the plain white strings still carry the heavier punishment when left out.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Leaving out the easy-to-get white strings is punished more than leaving out the hard-to-get תכלת.

steps.title: A person must say one hundred blessings every day
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר teaches that every person must say 100 ברכות a day, learning it from the פסוק ״מָה ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ שֹׁאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ״.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר used to say: A person must say one hundred ברכות every day, as the פסוק says: "And now, Israel, what does ה׳ your God ask of you."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third teaching of רבי מאיר, a daily obligation to say 100 ברכות, based on a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is a play on words: the word מָה (what) is read as if it were מֵאָה (one hundred). So the פסוק is read as saying that ה׳ asks of you one hundred, meaning 100 ברכות.

keyTerms.meaning: Asks of you, requires of you

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the well-known practice of saying 100 ברכות every day.

phrases.english: It is taught in a ברייתא: Rabbi Meir would say:
A person is obligated to recite
one hundred blessings every day,
as it is said: "And now, Israel,
what does ה׳ your God ask of you."
phrases.notes: דברים 10:12. He reads מָה (what) as if it said מֵאָה (one hundred).

steps.triggerLanguage: תניא, היה רבי מאיר אומר: חייב אדם לברך מאה ברכות בכל יום
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching of the same sage, רבי מאיר, on a different topic: daily ברכות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every person must say 100 ברכות each day.

steps.title: Filling up the hundred ברכות on שבת and יום טוב
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בריה דרב אויא would make an effort on שבת and יום טוב to reach 100 ברכות by eating spices and sweet fruits and making ברכות on them.
steps.simpleTranslation: On שבת and יום טוב, רב חייא the son of רב אויא would go out of his way to fill up the count of ברכות with ברכות on spices and sweet fruits.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story showing how one אמורא kept the rule of 100 ברכות even on days when it was harder to reach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On שבת and יום טוב the daily count falls short of 100. Instead of letting it go, רב חייא added ברכות by eating and smelling things that need their own ברכה. This shows how seriously the rule of רבי מאיר was taken in practice.

keyTerms.meaning: He made an effort, went out of his way

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר requires 100 ברכות a day, and רב חייא בריה דרב אויא worked hard to complete this count even on שבת and יום טוב.

phrases.english: Rav Chiya, son of Rav Avya,
on Shabbos and on Yom Tov,
would make an effort and fill them up
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the 100 ברכות. On these days the count comes up short, so he added more.

phrases.english: with spices and sweet fruits.

steps.triggerLanguage: רב חייא בריה דרב אויא בשבתא וביומי טבי טרח וממלי להו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the rule of 100 ברכות being put into practice on days when the count falls short.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even on שבת and יום טוב one should work to complete 100 ברכות, for example with ברכות on spices and fruits.

steps.title: רבי מאיר's three daily blessings
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר teaches that a person must say three ברכות every day: שלא עשאני גוי, שלא עשאני אשה, and שלא עשאני בור.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי מאיר used to say that a person must say three blessings every day: 'Who did not make me a gentile,' 'Who did not make me a woman,' and 'Who did not make me an ignoramus.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching of רבי מאיר. This one lists three specific ברכות a person must say every day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows straight from the last steps about ברכות, where רבי מאיר required 100 ברכות a day. Here he names three specific daily ברכות. The third one, שלא עשאני בור, is the one the next step will question.

keyTerms.meaning: Who did not make me a gentile
Who did not make me a woman
An ignorant person, someone without Torah knowledge

phrases.english: It is taught: Rabbi Meir would say:

phrases.aramaic: חַיָּיב אָדָם לְבָרֵךְ שָׁלֹשׁ בְּרָכוֹת בְּכׇל יוֹם,
phrases.english: A person is obligated to recite three blessings every day,
and these are: 'Who did not make me a gentile,'
'Who did not make me a woman,'
'Who did not make me an ignoramus.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of ברכות from רבי מאיר's 100 daily ברכות (step 20), now naming three specific daily ברכות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person must say three ברכות every day: שלא עשאני גוי, שלא עשאני אשה, שלא עשאני בור.

steps.title: רב אחא questions his son's blessing about not being an ignoramus
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר יעקב hears his son saying שלא עשאני בור and asks whether going this far is proper.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר יעקב heard his son saying the blessing 'Who did not make me an ignoramus.' He said to him: Even this much?
steps.whatsHappening: A short story: a father hears his son saying the ברכה of שלא עשאני בור and questions it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אחא challenges the third ברכה from רבי מאיר's list. He asks whether it is right to go 'this far' and thank ה׳ for not being a בור. This sets up the son's reply in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Even this much too? Asking whether something goes too far

phrases.aramaic: רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב שַׁמְעֵיהּ לִבְרֵיהּ
phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Yaakov heard his son
who was reciting the blessing 'Who did not make me an ignoramus.'
He said to him: Even this much too?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the third ברכה from רבי מאיר's list in step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The practice of saying שלא עשאני בור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Saying this ברכה seems to go too far, so it should not be said.

steps.title: The son asks what to say instead, since 'not a slave' equals 'not a woman'
steps.stepSummary: The son answers his father with a question: what else should be said? 'שלא עשאני עבד' would just repeat the ברכה about a woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: The son said to him: Then what blessing should one say? 'Who did not make me a slave'? That is the same as 'woman'!
steps.whatsHappening: The son defends his ברכה by asking what he should say in its place. He points out that the obvious replacement, 'not a slave,' would repeat a ברכה he already says.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son assumes three ברכות are needed. If שלא עשאני בור is dropped, the natural replacement is שלא עשאני עבד. But a slave is in the same category as a woman, so that would be the same ברכה said twice. That leaves no good third ברכה, so the son keeps שלא עשאני בור.

keyTerms.meaning: But then what? Asking for the alternative

phrases.english: He said to him: But then what blessing should one say?
phrases.notes: Now the son is speaking to his father.

phrases.english: 'Who did not make me a slave'?
That is the same as 'woman'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The son defends his practice against his father's question by challenging the alternative.
steps.kashyaTarget: Replacing שלא עשאני בור with שלא עשאני עבד
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שלא עשאני עבד would repeat שלא עשאני אשה, so it cannot be the third ברכה.

steps.title: רב אחא begins his answer: a slave
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא starts to answer his son with the word 'a slave'. The rest of his answer continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא answered: A slave...
steps.whatsHappening: The father starts his reply to his son's question. Only the first word, 'a slave', appears here, so the גמרא is setting up the rest of his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By opening with 'a slave', רב אחא is answering the son's claim that a slave is the same as a woman. He will explain why שלא עשאני עבד is still a separate ברכה, so the son should say it instead of שלא עשאני בור.

phrases.english: A slave...
phrases.notes: This is the father answering, and his sentence continues on the next line of the גמרא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב אחא begins to answer his son's claim that 'slave' is the same as 'woman'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The son thought a ברכה about a slave would just repeat the ברכה about a woman.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב אחא begins to show that a slave is different, so שלא עשאני עבד can be its own ברכה. His full answer comes next.
